## Question 5

### (a)
<!-- CREATE THE FUNCTION IN THE CODE CHUNK BELOW -->
<!-- NAME THE FUNCTION AND ITS INPUTS EXACTLY AS STATED IN THE ASSIGNENT -->
```{r Question 5a}
z_prop <- function(x, n, p0) {
  ((x / n) - p0) / sqrt((p0 * (1 - p0)) / n)
  
}

# p hat would be x/n here, since it is the proportion of successes out of all the trials, or sample proportion
```

### (b)
<!-- USE THE CODE CHUNK BELOW -->
```{r Question 5b}
z_prop(x = 10, n = 13, p0 = 0.6)
```

### (c)
<!-- ENTER YOUR ANSWER BELOW -->
A z-statistic of 1.245505 means that the sample that was observed is 1.245505 standard deviations above the mean.

### (d)
<!-- USE THE CODE CHUNK BELOW -->
```{r Question 5d}
z_prop(x = 30, n = 39, p0 = 0.6)
```
<!-- ENTER YOUR EXPLANATION BELOW -->
The z-statistic changes because although x/n, or the sample proportion or p hat, is still the same, the value of n in the denominator has changed. Because the n is in the denominator of the denominator, a higher value for n means a higher overall z-statistic.

## Question 6

### (a)
<!-- CREATE THE FUNCTION IN THE CODE CHUNK BELOW -->
<!-- NAME THE FUNCTION AND ITS INPUTS EXACTLY AS STATED IN THE ASSIGNENT -->
```{r Question 6a}
lease_calc <- function(msrp,
                       price,
                       down,
                       n = 36,
                       res = 0.60,
                       mf = 0.001,
                       tax = 0.095) {
  capitalized_cost <- price - down
  residual_value <- msrp * res
  monthly_depreciation <- (capitalized_cost - residual_value) / n
  monthly_finance_charge <- (capitalized_cost + residual_value) * mf
  sub_total <- monthly_depreciation + monthly_finance_charge
  sub_total + tax
}
```

### (b)
<!-- USE THE CODE CHUNK BELOW -->
```{r Question 6b}
lease_calc(msrp = 31495,
           price = 29895,
           down = 2500,
           res = 0.52,
           mf = 0.0016) 
```

I went in order from biggest to smallest coin (quarter, dime, nickel, penny) and calculated the largest number of that coin that could make up my current cents without going over. Starting with 47 cents, that would be one quarter, leaving me with 22 cents. 22 cents would be two dimes and 2 cents left over, which can only be two pennies.

### (b)

2. Integer division with remainder and 10 cents, if remainder is greater than 9. If not, skip.
2. Integer division with remainder and 5 cents, if remainder is greater than 4. If not, skip.

### (c)
<!-- CREATE THE FUNCTION IN THE CODE CHUNK BELOW -->
<!-- NAME THE FUNCTION AND ITS INPUTS EXACTLY AS STATED IN THE ASSIGNENT -->
```{r Question 7c}
get_minimum_coins <- function(cents) {
  q <- cents %/% 25
  d <- (cents - (25 * q)) %/% 10
  n <- (cents - (25 * q) - (10 * d)) %/% 5
  p <- (cents - (25 * q) - (10 * d) - (5 * n)) %/% 1
  
  q + d + n + p
}
```

### (d)
<!-- USE THE CODE CHUNK BELOW -->
```{r Question 6d}

get_minimum_coins(cents = 31)
get_minimum_coins(cents = 48)
get_minimum_coins(cents = 139)
```

(i) <!-- ENTER YOUR ANSWER TO THE RIGHT OF THIS OR BELOW -->
3 coins
(ii) <!-- ENTER YOUR ANSWER TO THE RIGHT OF THIS OR BELOW -->
6 coins
(iii) <!-- ENTER YOUR ANSWER TO THE RIGHT OF THIS OR BELOW -->
10 coins

### (e)
<!-- USE THE CODE CHUNK BELOW -->
```{r Question 6e}
get_minimum_coins(99)
```
<!-- ENTER YOUR EXPLANATION BELOW -->
It must be the number of cents that is not divisible by any of the coin amounts (5, 10, or 25). Each of the tens (10, 20, etc.) are divisible by 10, and anything above them would mean more coins. Therefore, I narrowed it down to 90-99. I excluded 100 since that would be simply 4 quarters. 90 coins would be 5 coins: 3 quarters, 1 dime, and 1 nickel. 91 coins would mean adding a penny (6), 92 another (7), 93 (8) up until 94 (9 coins). Similarly, 95 would be 5 coins, 96 - 6, 97- 7, 98 - 8 and 99 would be 9 coins. 99 is the number of cents less than 100 which requires the most coins.

## Question 8
<!-- THIS IS THE CODE GIVEN IN THE ASSIGNMENT -->
```{r Question 8 Background, echo = TRUE}
x <- 3
y <- 4
exp1 <- function() {
  x^y
}
exp2 <- function(x = 2) {
  x^y
}
exp_y <- function(x) {
  function(y) {
    x^y
  }
}
```

### (a)
<!-- ENTER YOUR ANSWER BELOW -->
Because in exp1(), the x value is the global x (3) since another is not defined, while in exp2() x is 2 since that is what x is defined as locally, or when the function is called. 

### (b)
<!-- ENTER YOUR ANSWER BELOW -->
It does not throw an error because x and y have values, as defined in the top of the cell (the global values) and R is able to access objects in the global environment within the local environment. 

### (c)
<!-- USE THE CODE CHUNK BELOW -->
```{r Question 8c}
exp_y(15)(4)

```
